prompt: Match each currency of estimation to what it is good at.

pairs.right: a date, if the guess is right

prompt: What condition must hold for counting items to work as a measure of size?

choices.text: Every item must be estimated first
choices.why: Counting needs no estimate at all.

choices.text: The team must use Kanban
choices.why: Any method can count its items.

choices.text: The team must have a year of history
choices.why: A few months of stable history is enough.

choices.text: Items are of broadly similar size
choices.why: Right. Which is met deliberately, by splitting.

prompt: Why is time, as a currency of estimation, a trap even when it is called a guess?

choices.text: Because nobody understands days
choices.why: Everybody understands them, which is the problem.

choices.text: It is heard as a promise, and leaves out waiting
choices.why: Right. An estimate of effort omits the queues where most time goes.

choices.text: Because time estimates are always too long
choices.why: They are usually too short.

choices.text: Because only points can be added up
choices.why: Days add up as easily as points.

prompt: Under the old rules, a one-point item took a median of 12 days. Why so long for the smallest estimate?

choices.text: Waiting dominated, at any size
choices.why: Right. Queues do not care how big an item is.

choices.text: One-point items were underestimated
choices.why: Their work was small; their waiting was not.

choices.text: Developers left small items for last
choices.why: billing.py picks items oldest first, regardless of size.

choices.text: Points are measured in weeks
choices.why: Points are relative and have no time unit.

prompt: The correlation between points and cycle time rose from 0.38 to 0.55 after 3 August. What does the lesson conclude?

choices.text: The team learned to estimate better
choices.why: The estimates come from the same rule throughout.

choices.text: Points became a reliable forecast for each item
choices.why: The groups still overlap a lot.

choices.text: The system changed; the points did not
choices.why: Right. The points did not get better; the system did.

choices.text: Correlations always rise over time
choices.why: Nothing makes them rise by themselves.

prompt: Under the new rules, the slowest one-point item took 5 days and the median three-point item took 5.5. By how many days did that median exceed the slowest one-pointer?
What does a correlation of 0 between points and days mean?

choices.text: Every item took zero days
choices.why: Correlation says nothing about the size of the values.

choices.text: Points and days rise together perfectly
choices.why: That is a correlation of 1.

choices.text: The program has failed
choices.why: Zero is a valid result.

choices.text: Points say nothing about days
choices.why: Right. They would have nothing to do with each other.

prompt: Why does points.py choose items by when they started rather than when they finished?

choices.text: Because finish dates are not recorded
choices.why: merged is recorded for every finished item.

choices.text: One set of rules per period
choices.why: Right. Items finishing in August include many started under the old rules.

choices.text: Because started items have more points
choices.why: Points do not depend on dates.

choices.text: Because it makes the correlation higher
choices.why: The reason is to compare like with like, not to raise a number.

prompt: Items varied by 31% week to week and points by 29%. What does that say about forecasting with points?

choices.text: It is no more precise than counting
choices.why: Right. And counting needs no meeting.

choices.text: Points are slightly better, so worth the meetings
choices.why: Two points of difference on eight weeks is noise.

choices.text: Neither can be used to forecast
choices.why: Both can; lesson 10 forecasts from the count.

choices.text: Points should be summed per developer
choices.why: That is lesson 8's trap.

prompt: The right-sizing question: can we finish this within our 85th ___?
A team finished 6, 9, 7 and 10 items in four weeks. What is its mean weekly throughput?
Why does right-sizing items also improve the delivery metrics of lessons 5 and 7?

choices.text: Because small items need no review
choices.why: Every item is reviewed.

choices.text: Because small items are counted twice
choices.why: Each counts once.

choices.text: Smaller items make smaller deployments
choices.why: Right. The batch-size argument from a different direction.

choices.text: Because points become more accurate
choices.why: Right-sized items need no points at all.

prompt: Why should a forecast leave out the first weeks after a change of rules?

choices.text: Because those weeks have the most points
choices.why: The point totals are not the reason.

choices.text: Because the team was on holiday
choices.why: Nothing in the history says so.

choices.text: Because the pipeline was down
choices.why: It deployed daily from 3 August.

choices.text: They contain the old system draining out
choices.why: Right. 13 items in the first week was July's queue, not the new rate.

prompt: What is #NoEstimates not?

choices.text: A conversation about whether every item needs an estimate
choices.why: That is exactly what it is.

choices.text: A refusal to give dates
choices.why: Right. Teams practising it forecast; they produce dates differently.

choices.text: A set of habits: split, count, forecast from history
choices.why: That is what it is in practice.

choices.text: Associated with Woody Zuill
choices.why: He started the hashtag in 2012.

prompt: What question does #NoEstimates ask of any practice, estimation included?

choices.text: Is a cheaper method as good?
choices.why: Right. For many decisions a count or a yes or no does as well.

choices.text: Who on the team estimates most accurately?
choices.why: That is a question about people, and not the one asked.

choices.text: How many points fit in a sprint?
choices.why: That presupposes the points.

choices.text: Which tool estimates automatically?
choices.why: Tools are not the subject.

prompt: A team stops estimating but keeps items whose sizes vary fiftyfold. What happens to its forecasts?

choices.text: They improve, because estimation bias is gone
choices.why: A count of wildly different items means little.

choices.text: They stay the same as with points
choices.why: Without splitting, the count loses what made it work.

choices.text: Nothing; forecasts do not depend on item size
choices.why: They depend on items being comparable.

choices.text: They get worse
choices.why: Right. The splitting is what makes #NoEstimates work.

prompt: Which situations does the lesson say are worth an estimate? Choose every one that applies.

choices.text: Deciding whether a piece of work is worth doing
choices.why: Right. An order of magnitude informs it well.

choices.text: Work unlike anything in the team's history
choices.why: Right. There is no history to count.

choices.text: A fixed-price contract signed before the work starts
choices.why: Right. Given as a range with a probability.

choices.text: Every item in every sprint, summed into a forecast
choices.why: That is the habit the lesson says rarely earns its cost.

prompt: What is taking the outside view, in Kahneman's sense?

choices.text: Asking an outside consultant for the estimate
choices.why: It is about where the evidence comes from, not who gives it.

choices.text: Reasoning forward from the plan step by step
choices.why: That is the inside view, which produces optimism.

choices.text: Starting from what happened to similar work
choices.why: Right. A reference class, in the team's past or elsewhere.

choices.text: Ignoring the team's opinion entirely
choices.why: The team chooses the reference class.

prompt: Two developers give the same item a one and an eight. What is the most useful thing about that?

choices.text: A misunderstanding to talk through
choices.why: Right. The disagreement is the useful output, and it needs no number written down.

choices.text: The average, 4.5, is a good estimate
choices.why: Averaging hides the misunderstanding.

choices.text: The higher estimate is the safe one
choices.why: Neither is safe until the gap is understood.

choices.text: It shows who is the better estimator
choices.why: That turns a conversation into a ranking.

prompt: A stakeholder asks how many points the team will deliver next quarter. What does the lesson suggest offering instead?

choices.text: A higher number of points, to show ambition
choices.why: Points summed into a forecast are no more precise than a count.

choices.text: An item forecast from history
choices.why: Right. Lesson 10 builds one.

choices.text: A refusal to answer
choices.why: A forecast is owed; only the method changes.

choices.text: Each developer's personal velocity
choices.why: Lesson 8's trap.

prompt: Put the #NoEstimates habits in the order a team applies them to new work.
items: split the work into small items
check each item fits the 85th percentile

prompt: A team finishes about 8 items a week and has 40 right-sized items to do. Ignoring variability, roughly how many weeks will they take?
hint: Lesson 10 shows why ignoring variability is not good enough.
